  MISSION STATEMENT
  The mission of the City of Monterey Park is to provide excellent services
  to enhance the quality of life for our entire community.

  LAND ACKNOWLEDGMENT
  We would like to acknowledge that the land we inhabit today was once known as
  Tovangaar, the home of the Gabrieleño-Tongva people. We show our respect to the
  Gabrieleño-Tongva people, as well as all Indigenous people, past, present, and future,
  and honor their labor as original caretakers of this land. We commit to uplifting the
  Gabrieleño-Tongva people, invite you to acknowledge the history, and join us in caring
  for this land.

GENERAL INFORMATION
Documents related to an Agenda item are available to the public in the City Clerk’s Office located at 320
West Newmark Avenue, Monterey Park, CA 91754, during normal business hours and the City’s website
at http://www.montereypark.ca.gov/AgendaCenter/City-Council-17.

The public may watch the meeting live on the city’s cable channel MPKTV (AT&T U-verse, channel 99
or Charter Communications, channel 182) or by visiting the city’s website at
http://www.montereypark.ca.gov/133/City-Council-Meeting-Videos. Per the Americans with Disabilities
Act, if you need special assistance to participate in this meeting, please call City Hall at (626) 307-1359
for reasonable accommodation at least 24 hours before a meeting. Council Chambers are wheelchair
accessible.

PUBLIC PARTICIPATION
You may speak up to 5 minutes on Agenda item. You may combine up to 2 minutes of time with another
person’s speaking. No person may speak more than a total of 10 minutes. The Mayor and City Council
may change the amount of time allowed for speakers. Written Communication will be accepted up to 24
hours before the meeting via email to mpclerk@montereypark.ca.gov.

While all comments are welcome, the Brown Act does not allow the City Council to take action on any
item not on the agenda. The Council may briefly respond to comments after Public Communications is
closed. Persons may, in addition to any other matter within the City Council's subject-matter jurisdiction,
comment on Agenda Items at this time. If you provide public comment on a specific Agenda item at this
time, however, you cannot later provide comments at the time the Agenda Item is considered.

  CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act):

  California Environmental Quality Act (Public Resources Code §§ 21000, et seq. “CEQA”) and

5-A.  CONSIDERATION AND POSSIBLE ACTION TO ADOPT AN URGENCY ORDINANCE

  FOUR-FIFTHS VOTE
  It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  (1) Adopting an Urgency Ordinance upon 4/5 vote pursuant to Government Code § 65858
  establishing a moratorium on new development within Saturn Park for 45 days; and
  (2) Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.
  CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act):
  Adopting the Urgency Ordinance is exempt from further environmental review under the
  California Environmental Quality Act (California Public Resources Code §§ 21000, et seq.,
  “CEQA”) and CEQA Guidelines (14 California Code of Regulations §§ 15000, et seq.) because
  it establishes rules and procedures for operation of existing facilities; minor temporary use of
  land; minor alterations in land use; new construction of small structures; and minor structures
  accessory to existing commercial facilities. The Urgency Ordinance, therefore, is categorically
  exempt from further CEQA review under CEQA Guidelines §§ 15301; 15303, 15304(e); 15305;
  and 15311. Further, the adoption of the Urgency Ordinance is also exempt from review under
  CEQA pursuant to CEQA Guidelines § 15061(b)(3) because the Ordinance is for general policies
  and procedure-making. This Ordinance does not authorize any new development entitlements,
  but simply establishes policies and procedures for allowing the previously approved project to
  be constructed. Any proposed project that will utilize the changes set forth in this Ordinance will
  be subject to CEQA review as part of the entitlement review of the project. The Ordinance will
  not adversely impact the environment and is therefore exempt from the provisions of CEQA.

2-A.  AWARD OF FRANCHISE AGREEMENTS FOR RESIDENTIAL  AND
  COMMERCIAL WASTE COLLECTION AND RECYCLING SERVICES

  On October 18, 2023, the City Council approved the release of a Request for
  Qualifications (RFQ) for residential and commercial waste collection and recycling
  services franchises. On January 17, 2024, City Council authorized the release of
  the Request for Application (RFA) and approved the list of companies that were
  qualified to submit proposals.

  The City received a total of five responses to the RFA, two applications for
  residential services from Athens Services and Ware Disposal and two applications
  for commercial services also from Athens Services and Ware Disposal. The three
  remaining companies withdrew from the process for various reasons. Should City
  Council opt for a three-cart collection system for residential waste collection and
  recycling services, the award of an exclusive residential franchise contract would
  be to Ware Disposal that submitted the lowest bid. However, if City Council
  chooses to continue with a two-cart system for residential services, the award of
  an exclusive residential franchise contract would be to Athens Services.

  Staff is requesting that the City Council award an exclusive franchise residential
  franchise to Ware Disposal for a three-cart system, or to Athens Services for a two-
  car system. Staff is also requesting that the City Council award non-exclusive
  commercial franchises to both Athens Services and Ware Disposal, or an exclusive
  commercial franchise to Ware – the lowest bidder.

  Page 11 of 459
   72-XXX

Athens proposed 49 exceptions to the residential and commercial agreements.
Should the City choose to award Athens a residential and/or commercial
agreement, City staff and Athens would need to resolve the proposed exceptions.
Ware proposed no exceptions to the residential and commercial agreements.

CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act):
The proposed actions for awarding solid waste franchises (the "Project") were
reviewed in accordance with the California Environmental Quality Act (Public
Resources Code §§ 21000, et seq., "CEQA") and the CEQA Guidelines (14
California Code of Regulations §§15000, et seq.). The Project is categorically
exempt from CEQA Guidelines § 15301 ("Existing Facilities") and § 15061(b)(3)
(the "Common Sense Exemption"). Moreover, none of the exceptions to the
categorical exemptions contained in CEQA Guidelines § 15300.2 are applicable to
the Project.

CEQA Guidelines § 15301 exempts

  "the operation, repair, maintenance, permitting, leasing, licensing, or
  minor alteration of existing public or private structure, facilities,
  mechanical equipment, or topographical features, involving
  negligible or no expansion of use beyond that existing at the time of
  the lead agency's determination."

Here, the City Council is contemplating the award of franchises for solid waste
collection, transportation, and recycling services. The franchises with the existing
solid waste service providers expire on August 31, 2024. MPMC Chapter 6.09
(approved by voters through Measure BB) generally requires that the City use a
competitive bidding process to choose solid waste service franchisees not later
than August 31, 2024. Pursuant to the MPMC, an exclusive franchise will be
awarded for residential accounts and up to three franchises may be awarded for
commercial accounts.

The services provided pursuant to the Project would be identical to, or substantially
the same as, that currently being provided throughout the City. Therefore, the
decision to approve the Project involves the operation and use of existing facilities
and equipment; it does not involve an expansion of use. Consequently, the Project
is exempt from additional environmental review pursuant to CEQA Guidelines §
15301.

CEQA Guidelines § 15061(b)(3) also exempts the Project from additional
environmental
review. That Section provides that

  "[w]here it can be seen with certainty that there is no possibility that
  the activity in question may have a significant effect on the
  environment, the activity is not subject to CEQA."

  Page 12 of 459
   72-XXX
  March 26, 2024

Here, the Project will not have a significant impact on the environment because
the future services will be identical to, or substantially the same as, the solid waste
collection, transportation and recycling services currently being provided. As is the
case with the current service provider, Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) powered
trash collection vehicles will be utilized. Therefore, no increases in air pollutants or
GHG emissions over the baseline conditions are expected. Vehicle routing will be
the same or substantially similar to that currently utilized and the City will retain the
power to approve all routes before the franchise periods begin. This will allow the
City to ensure that arterial streets and intersections with Level of Service (LOS)
issues can be avoided during peak hours.

Solid waste collection – now and in the future – may not commence before 7:00
a.m. or continue after 6:00 p.m. Solid waste franchisees must comply with MPMC
Chapter 9.53 which regulates noise. All vehicles will be subject to annual noise
level testing and certification by the City.

5-A.  BUSINESS ATTRACTION PROGRAM

  After dissolving redevelopment agencies, the California Legislature adopted
  “Economic Opportunity” legislation in 2014 which allows use of public funds to
  promote economic development (SB 470, Wright 2013). Depending on the type of
  economic development a city is seeking to promote, a city may be required to make
  findings to demonstrate that the development of the property is likely to create jobs,
  improve tax revenues, or satisfy a need for affordable housing. Additionally, cities
  may acquire, sell, or lease real property in furtherance of economic development
  (AB 806, Dodd and Frazier 2015).

  The City Council’s 2023-24 Strategic Plan includes a goal of Economic
  Development within the City. Utilizing elements of the Economic Opportunity
  legislation may help advance this goal.

  Action Taken: The City Council received and filed this report and provided
  directions to staff to explore other tools for integration into the next fiscal year’s
  budget.

2-A.  RESOLUTION REGARDING THE EXECUTION AND DELIVERY OF AN
  INSTALLMENT PURCHASE AGREEMENT FOR WATER REVENUE BONDS

  Issuing the proposed 2024 Water Revenue Bonds would allow the City to utilize
  $20.6 million in financing to replace aging infrastructure and install advanced water
  meter infrastructure. Consequently, the City Council may maintain the lower
  cumulative water rates approved in February 2024 and became effective March
  2024, instead of increasing such rates over the next five years. To implement the
  financing, the City would enter into an Installment Purchase Agreement with the
  Monterey Park Financing Authority the “Authority”), and the Authority would issue
  the 2024 Water Revenue Bonds in an amount not to exceed $22,000,000. Debt
  service will be repaid by the City from net revenues of the City’s water system.

  Discussion: Public Works Director Igoe and Finance Director Garcia, along with

2-B.  ADOPTION OF THE MONTEREY PARK SUSTAINABILITY PLAN

  The Plan outlines a comprehensive strategy aimed at fostering environmental
  stewardship and resilience within our community, aligning with California’s goals
  to combat climate change. The Plan suggests actions for individuals to enhance
  their sustainable practices while identifying strategic policies for City

  Page 33 of 459
   72-XX
  April 17, 2024
  implementation. Through a collaborative effort between stakeholders and City
  officials, the Plan announces the City’s commitment to mitigating emissions and
  advancing towards a greener future.

  Through the collaborative efforts of the Green Team which included a CivicSpark1
  fellow retained to lead this effort and various City employees/officials, the City
  prepared a draft Resolution and the Plan (contained in Attachments 1 and 2) for
  City Council consideration. A draft of the Plan was made available for public review
  between February 8 through 29, 2024. Public outreach was conducted during this
  period to solicit input and comments. The Implementation Program, contained in
  Attachment 3 to the staff report, is included as informational only and will guide the
  City’s implementation actions should the Plan be adopted.

  CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act):
  The City reviewed the environmental impacts of the proposed Resolution pursuant
  to the California Environmental Quality Act (Public Resources Code §§ 21000, et
  seq. “CEQA”) and the regulations promulgated thereunder (14 Cal. Code of Regs.
  §§ 15000, et seq., the “CEQA Guidelines”). CEQA Guidelines §§ 15060(c)(2),
  15061(b)(3), 15378, and 15308 exempt activities that will not result in a direct or
  reasonably foreseeable indirect physical change in the environment, activities
  where there is possibility that it may have a significant effect on the environment,
  activities that do not constitute a “project” as defined, and actions to protect the
  environment, respectively. This activity is for general policies and procedure-
  making intended to promote environmental sustainability and protect the
  environment. Any subsequent construction or development will be evaluated
  separately under the CEQA Guidelines. Accordingly, this Resolution is exempt
  from further review.

  Discussion: Director of Community Services Serrano and CivicSpark Fellow
  Williams, along with Hannah Mize, Sustainability Project Manager at Rincon
  Consultants, Inc. who was virtually present, presented a PowerPoint presentation
  on the Sustainability Plan and were available for questions.

  Action Taken: The City Council adopted Resolution No. 2024-R22 to adopt the
  Monterey Park Sustainability Plan (the “Plan”).

 SUBJECT:  Adoption of Fiscal Year 2024-25 Annual Budget

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Adopting by Resolution the City’s and Successor Agency’s Fiscal Year 2024-
  2025 Annual Budget as presented on May 22, 2024;
  2. Adopting a Resolution approving the Citywide Combined Salary Schedule; and
  3. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
On May 22, 2024, the City Council conducted a public budget workshop regarding the
City’s current finances, projected revenues, financial obligations, and proposed budget
for fiscal year 2024-25. The budget for FY 2024-2025 presents a spending plan that
anticipates $167.9 million in estimated operating revenues and transfers-in; $9.5 million
from grant advancements and fund balance from all funds combined; and $177.4 million
in operating, and capital improvements expenditures and transfers-out. Significant
changes to next fiscal year’s budget including the addition of one staff, the completion of
American Rescue Program Act (ARPA) funding, the increased Unfunded Accrual Liability
(UAL), and all other goals and objectives associated with the City budget, were presented
and discussed at the workshop.
In addition, the City Council’s fiscal year 2024-2025 Strategic Plan Goals were added to
the budget document to provide a roadmap for prioritizing implementation of the specific
objectives that will be focused on during the budget cycle.

BACKGROUND:
Strategic planning is a method by which the City Council plans and prioritizes its goals in
a transparent and accountable manner. At a public meeting held on February 3, 2024, the
City Council and City’s management team met to discuss fiscal year 2024-2025 City
Council priorities and strategic plan goals. The Strategic Plan goals enable the City to
efficiently move the community forward by focusing on specific objectives during the
fiscal year. The Strategic Plan goals can be found on pages B12-B14 (and are also listed
below) of the fiscal year 2024-25 budget book. The Plan aligns limited resources with
prioritized initiatives, which connect to a broader vision for our community’s future.

On May 22, 2024, City Council conducted a public budget workshop wherein FY 2024-25
estimated revenues presented were $167.9 million, grant advancements and fund
balance were $9.5 million, and expenditures were $177.4 million. The workshop included
discussions on the addition of staff to the City’s employee roster, the American Rescue
Program Act funds and general fund supplement, the City’s current CalPERs Unfunded
Accrual Liability, employee salary and benefit increases per bargaining unit
Memorandums of Understanding, and all other goals and objectives associated with the
City budget.
The FY 2024-2025 proposed budget includes cost increases for salary and benefits per
bargaining unit Memoranda of Understanding. The attached combined salary schedule
will take affect the first full pay period after July 1, 2024.

Therefore, the City’s FY 2024-2025 Operating, Debt and Capital Budget total is $177.4
million of which $65.7 million is in the General Fund, $24.5 million is for capital
improvements and $2.2 is for the Successor Agency enforceable obligations and
administration costs. A careful and methodical approach was taken in preparing the
budget consistent with City Council’s practice to exercise fiscal prudence with funding
requests and the preservation of the General Fund reserves. Departmental budget
requests were scrutinized considering essential operational needs and limiting the
ongoing demand on the City’s finances. This operating budget takes the stance of status
quo with escalations only where the cost-of-service delivery has increased and where a
need for additional services has been identified.
FISCAL IMPACT:
The FY 2024-2025 citywide budget is estimated to be $177.4 million, with a General Fund
Budget of $65.7 million (net of transfers).

  DATE: June 18, 2024
  AGENDA ITEM NO: Consent Calendar - 3D

 TO:  The Honorable Mayor and City Council
 FROM:  Kristin Olivarez, City Librarian
 SUBJECT:  Waive Library Card Replacement Fee for Library Card Sign-up Month

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Waiving the library card replacement fee for library patrons for the month of
  September 2024 in celebration of National Library Card Sign-up Month;
  2. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
It is recommended that City Council waive the library card replacement fee during the
month of September 2024 in celebration of National Library Card Sign-up Month. There
is no fee to register for a library card. If a library card is lost, patrons are charged a fee to
replace their card. Free library card replacement will encourage residents of all ages to
return to the Library and utilize the variety of services and programs available to them,
including the Library’s physical collections, public computers, teen, adult and children’s
programming, online resources, English as a Second Language classes and more. This
action will align with the Library’s Strategic Plan goal of making it easier and more
convenient for every resident to use the Library.

Additionally, in March 2024, the Library released two new library card designs created by
Monterey Park residents. Waiving the card replacement fee will also help promote the
new library cards and allow library patrons to replace their old card with one of the new
designs.

Since 1987, Library Card Sign-up Month has been held each September to mark the
beginning of the school year. During the month, the American Library Association and
libraries unite in a national effort to encourage everyone to register for a free card at their
local public library.

FISCAL IMPACT:
The library card replacement fee is $3.10. Based on FY 2023/24 data, the library card
replacement fee generates an average revenue of $24 per month.

SUBJECT:  A Resolution Declaring the Month of July as “Parks Make Life Better”
  Month in the City of Monterey Park

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:

  1. Adopting a Resolution declaring the month of July as “Parks Make Life Better”
  Month in the City of Monterey Park; and
  2. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
During July, the Recreation and Community Services Department celebrates "Parks
Make Life Better” month. By designating July as "Parks Make Life Better" month, the
City of Monterey Park, Recreation and Community Services Department urges all
residents to enjoy and recognize our parks' social, physical, mental, economic,
environmental, and community benefits. As we observe "Parks Make Life Better" month,
we recognize the vital contributions of our employees and volunteers, who all contribute
to making parks and recreation facilities a great place to visit. These dedicated staff and
volunteers keep our parks clean and safe for visitors and coordinate and organize
special events, childcare, summer day camp, swim lessons, educational classes, senior
activities, and health and fitness programs. They ensure that parks and recreation
facilities are safe and accessible places to enjoy.

BACKGROUND:
The National Recreation and Park Association (NRPA) and California Parks and
Recreation Society (CPRS) are organizations dedicated to advancing park, recreation,
and conservation efforts that enhance the quality of life for all people. The NRPA and
CPRS encourage promoting healthy lifestyles, recreation initiatives, and conservation of
natural and cultural resources. Since 1985, the NRPA and CPRS have recognized July
as "Parks Make Life Better” month in California and nationally as "Parks and
Recreation" month. Cities, counties, and other agencies recognize the importance of
thriving local park systems as providing an opportunity for all people to lead healthy,
active lifestyles and the preservation of great community places.

 SUBJECT:  Authorize the City Manager to Amend Agreement No. 1718-A with World

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Authorizing the City Manager to amend agreement no. 1718-A and extend the
  term for an additional five years;
  2. Amend agreement no. 1718-A, Article 2.2 to reflect an annual reimbursement
  from World Journal to the City in the amount of $10,000 to offset the cost of City
  staffing and services in a form approved by the City Attorney, with World Journal
  LA, LLC to co-produce the Monterey Park Lunar New Year Festival; and
  3. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
The City of Monterey Park has cohosted the annual Lunar New Year Festival with World
Journal LA, LLC since 2012. In April 2024, Agreement no. 1718-A between the City of
Monterey Park and World Journal LA, LLC (World Journal) ended its term. City staff has
been satisfied with World Journal’s performance since 2012 and recommends extending
the term and adjusting the reimbursed amount in article 2.2 of the agreement.

Due to continued incidents of gun violence throughout the nation, over the years there
has been a necessity to strengthen and increase safety personnel, leading to additional
costs incurred for city staffing and services. This event attracts many attendees and is
free and open to all, which requires extensive planning and adequate levels of safety
staffing. On June 5, 2024, the City Council authorized City staff to negotiate with World
Journal and update the agreement term and article 2.2 to increase the amount reimbursed
to the city to help offset the cost of city staffing and services.

City staff has met with the World Journal, which has agreed to increase the amount
identified in Article 2.2 with a reimbursement of $10,000 per year to offset the cost of City
staffing and services.

BACKGROUND:
The City’s Annual Lunar New Year Festival is located on East Garvey Avenue in the
downtown area from Garfield Avenue to Alhambra Avenue. The event features
entertainment, food, and over 200 commercial vendors and cultural booths. Attendance
for the two-day event is estimated to be approximately 200,000 attendees each year.

The Business Improvement District Advisory Committee (BIDAC) and City staff have
expressed satisfaction with the collaborative efforts with World Journal since the inaugural
event in 2012. The event attracts attendees from near and far to celebrate and shop
throughout the city. It is unfeasible to calculate the dollar value that the annual festival
generates for the City’s local economy. However, the City’s partnership with World
Journal is valued as a collaborative endeavor to host this traditional, family-friendly event
that the community continues to enjoy each year.

Building on this successful partnership, the event will continue among the World Journal,
the City, and the BIDAC. World Journal will retain the responsibilities for vendor and
sponsor recruitment, securing essential services for equipment rental, waste
management, and restroom facilities, as well as coordinating entertainment, decor,
marketing, security, and all other financial and logistical obligations resulting from the
event's production. The BIDAC will collaborate with the City to organize the Opening
Ceremony and engage with local businesses in the area impacted by the two-day event.

FISCAL IMPACT:
City staffing and services cost approximately $77,000 annually, including public safety,
street closures, inspections, traffic, and other safety-related duties. World Journal has
agreed to pay $10,000 to the City to offset the costs of staffing and services. In addition,
which is not described in the agreement, the City also collects $75 for each vendor that
does not have a current Monterey Park business license for an estimated $9,000 per
year.

 TO:  The Honorable Mayor and City Council
 FROM:  Shawn Igoe, Director of Public Works
 SUBJECT:  Authorize Purchase of a Fuel Delivery/Control System

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Waiving the bidding requirements pursuant to Monterey Park Municipal Code
  Section 3.20.050(3) and (4), and authorizing the City Manager to purchase an
  OPW Fuel Management System at the cost of $140,458.93;
  2. Approving an appropriation of $140,459 from Shop Fund 501 for this purchase;
  and
  3. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
The Public Works Fleet Maintenance Division is seeking to replace their current fuel
management and delivery system, GasBoy. This system is over 20 years old and is no
longer serviceable. The operating system firmware, software, and hardware are no longer
repairable or supported by any known vendor. A portion of the fueling system is currently
inoperable, creating operational challenges for fueling vehicles. Public Works seeks City
Council approval for the purchase of a replacement fuel management and delivery
system, OPW sold by Orange Coast Petroleum Equipment, Inc. The OPW system was
identified through a Sourcewell contract.

BACKGROUND:
The Fleet Maintenance Division solicited quotes from local known vendors for an updated
and modern management system for fuel tracking and delivery. The City is seeking a
system with a stand-alone pedestal pump system for three City locations that could be
integrated with the new FASTER ASSET fleet software management system, which was
awarded by the City Council at its February 21, 2023 meeting, and with all vehicles within
the City fleet inventory.

OPW emerged as the most reliable industry standard, and universally readable system
on the West coast. Orange Coast Petroleum Equipment, Inc. offered the requested
system at Sourcewell pricing. The proposed OPW system would replace the three City
GasBoy systems at the City Yard (City vehicle use), City Yard (public CNG), and Fire
Station #1.

  Page 157 of 459
 Staff Report
June 18, 2024
Page 2 of 3

The OPW system features include hosted software and bank card processing, wireless
Automatic Vehicle Identification (AVI), passive vehicle tagging that would enable the City
to track vehicle usage efficiency, auto mileage reading, theft reconciliation capability, high
/ low temperature advisories, and real-time inventory data storage and reporting. This
system also provides options to record and transmit traffic related diagnostic data via
GPS.

The City is a member of Sourcewell, a purchasing cooperative that combines the
purchasing power of multiple agencies into a cooperative purchasing group to secure
lower prices than what a smaller agency may obtain through an individual bid. Sourcewell
contracts are competitively solicited and meet public bidding processes; accordingly, the
City Council may authorize purchase of the OPW Fuel Management System via MPMC
§ 3.20.050(3) and (4) – which allows the City to forego bidding when it is in the City’s best
interests. Staff is recommending that the City Council utilize these provisions because the
quote received from Orange Coast Petroleum Equipment was the best value and because
Orange Coast Petroleum Equipment’s quote came via the Sourcewell purchasing
cooperative. The total cost of the new system is $140,458.93. Annual recurring fees for
the system are $3,720. It is recommended that City Council approve the purchase of the
OPW Fuel Delivery/Control System through Orange Coast Petroleum Equipment, Inc.

FISCAL IMPACT:
The total purchase cost is $140,458.93. An appropriation of $140,459 from Shop Fund
501 is required for this purchase. Annual subscription fees will be budgeted as part of the
annual budget process.

 TO:  The Honorable Mayor and City Council
 FROM:  Shawn Igoe, Director of Public Works
 SUBJECT:  Resolution Identifying a Public Works Street Maintenance Project to be
  Included in the FY 2024-25 Budget and Funded by Senate Bill 1: The
  Road Repair and Accountability Act of 2017

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Adopting a resolution identifying a street maintenance project to be included in the
  FY 2024-25 budget and funded with Road Maintenance and Rehabilitation Act
  (RMRA) funds, in a form approved by the City Attorney; and
  2. Take such additional, related action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
Senate Bill 1 (SB1), the Road Repair and Accountability Act of 2017, addresses the
significant multi-modal transportation funding shortfall statewide. As of November 2017,
portions of SB1 revenues are deposited into a Road Maintenance and Rehabilitation
Account (RMRA) and made available to eligible cities and counties, which must comply
with RMRA funding requirements as determined by the California Transportation
Commission (CTC).

RMRA funds made available for the Local Streets and Roads Funding Program are
prioritized for expenditure on basic road maintenance and rehabilitation projects, and on
critical safety projects. The CTC provided a number of example projects and uses for
RMRA funding that includes, but are not limited to, the following: road maintenance and
rehabilitation, safety projects, railroad grade separations, complete streets components
(including active transportation purposes, pedestrian and bicycle safety projects, transit
facilities, and drainage and stormwater capture projects in conjunction with any other
allowable project), and traffic control devices.

BACKGROUND:
The most recent State estimates for FY 2024-25 project Monterey Park will receive
$1,461,806 in RMRA funds. In order to be eligible to receive these funds, agencies must
submit a proposed project list to the CTC by July 1, 2024, along with budget support
documentation including the meeting minutes and/or resolution of the City Council
committing to the project list. This year, project lists are due July 1, 2024.

  Page 181 of 459

The proposed resolution and project list includes the resurfacing and rehabilitation of
various local streets as identified in the City’s Pavement Management Study. Staff
reviewed the study and selected those street segments that would most benefit from a
rehabilitation project based on their current conditions. Once the resolution is adopted and
submitted, staff may begin the design. Once plans and specifications are complete,
construction of the project is expected to be completed by Spring of 2025. The proposed
rehabilitation work consists primarily of grinding and overlay of the roadway surface with
asphalt concrete and asphalt rubber hot mix.

FISCAL IMPACT:
As the City’s budget process for FY 2024-25 is now underway, the adoption of the
resolution to include the capital improvement project in the upcoming budget and funded
with RMRA funds will allow the City to receive the RMRA funding for street rehabilitation
projects, and help the City improve the overall quality of its roadway system.

CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act):
The City reviewed the environmental impacts of the proposed Ordinance pursuant to the
California Environmental Quality Act (Public Resources Code §§ 21000, et seq. “CEQA”)
and the regulations promulgated thereunder (14 Cal. Code of Regs. §§ 15000, et seq.,
the “CEQA Guidelines”). CEQA Guideline § 15301(c) (Existing Facilities) exempts the
operation, repair, maintenance, alteration of existing public or private structures which
involve negligible or no expansion of existing or former use. The proposed work will occur
entirely within an existing structure. Accordingly, no further environmental review is
required.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Capital Improvement Project (“CIP”) No. 95013 & 95014 – Langley Senior Citizen Center
and Barnes Park Gymnasium Restroom Rehabilitation Project includes the rehabilitation
of the restrooms at the Langley Senior Center and Barnes Park Gymnasium restrooms.
Pursuant to Resolution No. 2023-R52, the Public Works Director solicited bids for the
restroom rehabilitation at Langley Senior Citizen Center and Barnes Park Gymnasium
(Specification No. 2024-003).

The public bid opening for the Langley Senior Citizen Center and Barnes Park
Gymnasium Restrooms Rehabilitation project was held on May 24, 2024. One bid was
received: U.S. Builders and Consultants Inc. As required by HUD for the use of CDBG
funds, staff held a pre-bid meeting and was attended by 2 potential bidders including U.S.

 User Fee Background
Policy Considerations
User Fees recover costs associated with the providing specific services benefiting the user, thereby typically
reducing the use of General Fund monies for such purposes.
In addition to collecting the direct cost of labor and materials associated with processing and administering
user services, it is common for local governments to recover reasonable support costs. Support costs are
those costs relating to a local government’s central service departments that are allocable to the local
government’s operating departments. Central services support cost allocations were incorporated using
the resulting indirect overhead percentages determined through the City’s Cost Allocation Plan. This plan
was used in the User Fee study to account for the burden placed upon central services by the operating
departments in order to allocate a proportionate share of central service cost through the study.
As labor effort and costs associated with the provision of services fluctuate over time, a significant element
in the development of any fee schedule is that it has the flexibility to remain current. Therefore, it is
recommended that the City include an inflationary factor in the resolution adopting the fee schedule to
allow the City Council, by resolution, to annually increase or decrease the fees.
The City may employ many different inflationary factors. The most commonly used inflator is some form
of Consumer Price Index (“CPI”) as it is widely well known and accepted. A similar inflator is the implicit
price deflator for Gross Domestic Product (“GDP”), which is much like the CPI except that while the CPI is
based on the same “basket” of goods and services every year, the price deflators’ “basket” can change year
to year. Since the primary factor for the cost of a City’s services is usually the costs of the personnel
involved, tying an inflationary factor that connects more directly to the personnel costs can also be suitable
if there is a clear method, or current practice of obtaining said factor.
Each City should use an inflator that they believe works the best for their specific situation and needs. It is
also recommended that the City perform this internal review annually with a comprehensive review of
services and fees performed every five years, which would include adding, amending, or removing fees for
programs/services.

 Project Approach and Methodology
Conceptual Approach
The basic concept of a User Fee Study is to determine the “reasonable cost” of each service provided by
the City for which it charges a User Fee. The full cost of providing a service may not necessarily become the
City’s fee, but it serves as the objective basis as to the maximum amount that may be collected.
The standard fee limitation established in California law for such fees is the “estimated, reasonable cost”
principle. In order to maintain compliance with the letter and spirit of this standard, every component of
the fee study process included a related review. The use of budget figures, time estimates, and
improvement valuation clearly indicates reliance upon estimates for some data.

Fully Burdened Hourly Rates
The total cost of each service included in this analysis is primarily based on the Fully Burdened Hourly Rates
(“FBHRs”) that were determined for City personnel directly involved in providing services. The FBHRs
include not only personnel salary and benefits, but also any costs that are reasonably ascribable to
personnel. The cost elements that are included in the calculation of fully burdened rates are:
    Salaries & benefits of personnel involved
    Operating costs applicable to fee operations
    Departmental support, supervision, and administration overhead
    Indirect City-wide overhead costs calculated through the Cost Allocation Plan
An important factor in determining the fully burdened rate is in the calculation of productive hours for
personnel. This calculation takes the available workable hours in a year of 2,080 and adjusts this figure to
1,650 productive or billable hours to account for calculated or anticipated hours’ employees are involved
in non-billable activities such as paid vacation, sick leave, holidays, and other considerations as necessary.
Dividing the full cost, including overhead, of a position by the number of productive hours provides the
FBHR.
The FBHRs are then used in conjunction with time estimates, when appropriate for how a service is
provided, to calculate a fee’s cost based on the personnel and the amount of their time that is involved in
providing each service.

 Methodology
The three methods of analysis for calculating fees used in this report are the:

Case Study Method (Standard Unit Cost Build-Up Approach): This approach estimates the actual
labor and material costs associated with providing a unit of service to a single user. This analysis is suitable
when City staff time requirements do not vary dramatically for a service, or for special projects where the
time and cost requirements are easy to identify at the project’s outset. Further, the method is effective in
instances when a staff member from one department assists on an application, service or permit for
another department on an as-needed basis. Costs are estimated based upon interviews with City staff
regarding the time typically spent on tasks, a review of available records, and a time and materials analysis.

Programmatic Approach: In some instances, the underlying data is not available or varies widely, leaving
a standard unit cost build-up approach impractical. In addition, market factors and policy concerns (as
opposed to actual costs) tend to influence rental based fee levels more than other types of services. Willdan
employed a different methodology where appropriate to fit a programs’ needs and goals. Typical
programmatic approach cases are facility use fees, penalties, and instances where a program cost is divided
over the user base to obtain a per applicant cost for shared cost services.

Valuation Based Fees: This manner of collection is used when the valuation of the improvement can be
used as a proxy for the amount of effort it would take for City staff to complete the service provided. More
specifically, this approach is commonly used for certain User Fees in the Building Division. It is generally
accepted that as a project’s size scales up, the cost of the project increases, and the amount of effort needed
to review and inspect also increases. Using a valuation-based fees provides for a system that can adjust as
project sizes scale. Land is not included in the valuation.

Cost Recovery
The cost recovery models, by department/division fee type, are presented in detail in Appendix C. Full cost
recovery is determined by summing the estimated amount of time each position (in increments of minutes
or hours) spends to render a service. Time estimates for each service rendered were obtained through
interviews conducted with City staff for each department/division fee included in the study. The resulting
cost recovery amount represents the total cost of providing each service. The City’s current fee being
charged for each service, if applicable, is provided in this section, as well, for reference.
It is important to note that the time data used to determine the amount of time each employee spends
assisting in the provision of the services listed on the fee schedule is essential in identifying the total cost
of providing each service, and will differ from City to City depending on staffing, positions involved,
experience on staff, the use of consultants, and the policies and procedures in place for each City.
Specifically, in providing services, a number of employees are often involved in various aspects of the
process, spending anywhere from a few minutes to several hours on the service.
The primary goal of this study was to identify the cost of City services, to provide information to help the
City make informed decisions regarding the actual fee levels and charges. The responsibility of determining
the final fee levels is a complicated task. City staff must consider many issues in formulating
recommendations, and the City Council must consider those same issues and more in making the final
decisions.
City staff assumes the responsibility to develop specific fee level recommendations to present to the City
Council. Unfortunately, there are no fixed rules to guide the City, since many of the considerations are based
on the unique characteristics of the City of Monterey Park, and administrative and political discretion.
However, in setting the level of full cost recovery for each fee, one should consider whether the service
solely benefits one end user or the general community.

Subsidization
The general concept for a user fee is that individuals (or groups) who receive a private benefit should pay
100% of the full cost of services provided to that individual (or group) that is separate from the general
public. Services that are a public benefit should be funded entirely by the general fund’s tax dollars.
Unfortunately, for the decision makers, some services fall into the range between these two extremes.
Of course, subsidization can be an effective public policy tool, since it can be used to reduce fees to
encourage certain activities (such as to ensure public safety) or allow some people to be able to afford to
receive services they otherwise could not at the full cost. In addition, subsidies can be an appropriate and
justifiable action, such as to allow citizens to rightfully access services, without overburdensome costs.
Despite the intent, it is important for the City and public to understand that subsidies must be paid for by
another revenue source, typically the General Fund’s other unobligated funds. Therefore, the general
taxpayer will potentially help to fund private benefits, and/or other City services will not have available
funds that are otherwise directed to cover fee subsidies.

 Impact on Demand (Elasticity)
Economic principles of elasticity suggest that increased costs for services (or higher fees) will eventually
curtail the demand for the services; whereas lower fees may spark an incentive to utilize the services and
encourage certain actions. Either of these results may be desirable to the City. However, the level of the
fees that would cause demand changes is largely unknown. The cost of service study did not attempt to
evaluate the economic or behavioral impacts of higher or lower fees; nevertheless, the City should consider
the potential impacts of these issues when deciding on fee levels.

recreation services. The fee for use of government owned facilities and property can be set discretionally
by the City per Proposition 26 to reduce the cost to the public for related facilities costs, and because there
is market availability for facility use elsewhere. The cost of acquisition, maintenance, repair, and upgrade
to the City and subsequently the community is partially offset by rental or use fee revenue. These fees
should be set using the knowledge of activity use for the facilities, policy desires of the City, and market
factors when desirable. It is generally accepted that many Recreation programs provide a measure of public
benefit to the residents and City as a whole. In addition, cities generally want to ensure that their programs
and services remain affordable to the community at large, and that the programs remain competitive with
surrounding jurisdictions and private businesses. Therefore, full cost recovery is typically not the primary
goal of fee setting. Reasonable estimates for time for direct staff involvement on each fee were used in a
cost analysis to determine direct staff fully burdened cost. The analysis found that all fees are currently set
well below the direct staff's fully burdened cost of service. The department Director is suggesting
reasonable fee adjustments to the fee schedule, as detailed in Appendix C. As a result, there would be:

    An increase for 53 fees;
    3 new fees would be added;
    4 fees would remain as currently set; and
    Average fee change would be around a 17% increase and would maintain an average subsidy level
  of 65% for listed fees.

   RESOLUTION NO.

  A RESOLUTION ADOPTING A FEE SCHEDULE TO RECOVER COSTS
  INCURRED FROM PROVIDING VARIOUS PUBLIC SERVICES.

The City Council of the City of Monterey Park does resolve as follows:

SECTION 1: The City Council finds as follow:

  A. The City Council may establish fees for services under various provisions
  of California law including, without limitation, Business & Professions Code
  § 16000; Government Code §§ 54344, 65104, 65909.5, 65943, 66013,
  66014, 66451.2; and Health & Safety Code §§ 17951, 17980.1, and 19852;

  B. Pursuant to Government Code § 66016, the City made data available
  regarding the cost, or estimated cost, of providing certain municipal services
  for the proposed user fees 10 days before the public hearing held on June
  18th, 2024;

  C. On June 18th, 2024, the City Council heard public testimony and considered
  evidence in a public hearing held and noticed in accordance with
  Government Code §§ 66016 and 66018; and

  D. After careful consideration, including a review of the documentary and
  testimonial evidence submitted during the public hearing, the City Council
  finds that the user fees adopted by this Resolution are in the public interest
  to recover the costs of certain municipal services.

SECTION 2: The Fees, attached as Exhibit “A,” and incorporated into this Resolution as
if fully set forth, are approved, and adopted.

SECTION 3: Unless otherwise revised, the fees established by this Resolution will be
automatically adjusted on an annual basis on July 1 of each year by applying the percent
change of the Los Angeles Area of Consumer Price Index (CPI) for All Urban Consumers
for the prior 12 month period ending on April 30 to the City’s costs for administering the
services set forth in Exhibit “A.” The first fee adjustment cannot be made before a
minimum of nine months after the effective date of this Resolution.

SECTION 4: This Resolution is exempt from review under the California Environmental
Quality Act (Cal. Pub. Res. Code §§ 21000, et seq.; “CEQA”) and CEQA Guidelines (14
Cal. Code Regs. §§ 15000, et seq.) because it establishes, modifies, structures,
restructures, and approves rates and charges for meeting operating expenses;
purchasing supplies, equipment, and materials; meeting financial requirements; and
obtaining funds for capital projects needed to maintain service within existing service
areas. This Resolution, therefore, is categorically exempt from further CEQA review under
CEQA Guidelines § 15273.

 FROM:  Shawn Igoe, Director of Public Works
 SUBJECT:  Resolution for the FY2024-25 Capital Improvement Plan

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Opening a public hearing to receive documentary and testimonial evidence;
  2. After closing the public hearing and considering the evidence, adopting a
  Resolution finding the FY2024-25 Capital Improvement Plan (“CIP”) conforms with
  the General Plan, Authorizing the City Engineer to approve plans and
  specifications for capital improvement projects, and authorizing the Public Works
  Director to solicit bids for capital improvement projects identified in the CIP; and
  3. Taking such additional, related action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
The City’s FY2024-25 proposed budget includes an updated Capital Improvement Plan
(“CIP”) outlining the City’s capital investments over a five-year period. Staff asks that the
City Council adopts of a Resolution to approve the proposed CIP, grants authorization for
the City Engineer to approve plans specifications for Capital Improvement Projects, and
authorizes for the Director of Public Works to advertise projects for construction bids when
required or needed.

BACKGROUND
The CIP generally identifies which capital improvement projects will be built during a five-
year period; it is updated annually and approved by the City Council. The CIP includes
major enhancements and repairs to critical public assets, including parks, City-owned
facilities, streets, traffic signals, storm drains, sidewalks, bus stops, transportation, water
and sewer facilities. Completion of CIP projects helps to enhance the overall quality of life
in the City by improving the physical structures, systems, and facilities that provide
services to the community. The Public Works Department is responsible for implementing
the City’s CIP. Each year, Public Works, in conjunction with other Departments, reviews
the City’s capital needs and prioritizes projects through the annual budget process.

It is recommended that the City Council adopt a resolution approving the proposed FY
2024-25 CIP list of projects. If the proposed Resolution is adopted, the CIP will be
approved; the City Engineer will be authorized to approve plans/specifications (for design
immunity purposes); and the Public Works Director will be authorized to solicit bids for
CIP projects.

  PLAN (“CIP”) CONFORMS WITH THE GENERAL PLAN; AUTHORIZING

  IMPROVEMENT PROJECTS IDENTIFIED IN THE CIP.

  The City Council of the city of Monterey Park does resolve as follows:

SECTION 1: Planning Agency. Pursuant to Monterey Park Municipal Code (“MPMC”) §
2.56.020(B), the City Council is the Monterey Park Planning Agency for purposes of this
Resolution. In accordance with Government Code § 65401, the Public Works Director
prepared and submitted a capital improvement plan (“CIP”) to the Planning Agency as
set forth in attached Exhibit “A,” which is incorporated by reference. Government Code §
65103(C) requires the Planning Agency to annually review the City’s CIP to determine
whether the CIP is consistent with the Monterey Park General Plan. The City Council
finds that the CIP is consistent with the Monterey Park General Plan. Among other things
the CIP meets the following goals in the General Plan:

  •  Goal 2.0 of the Circulation Element: Provide a local street system that
  accommodates current and future traffic volumes;

  •  Goal 5.0 of the Circulation Element: Create and maintain a connected
  system of bicycle routes and pedestrian facilities that meets the need of City
  residents;

  •  Goal 6.0 of the Circulation Element: Ensure that all development projects
  provide well-designed parking facilities that are safe, convenient, and
  attractive;

  •  Goal 3.0 of the Safety and Community Services Element: Protect public and
  private properties from geologic hazards associated with steep slopes,
  unstable hillsides, and liquefaction-prone areas;

  •  Goal 13.0 of the Safety and Community Services Element: Provide
  adequate sewer, water, and drainage systems to meet the needs of City
  residents and businesses; and

  •  Goal 4.0 of the Resources Element: Conserve and protect groundwater
  supply and water resources.

SECTION 2: Design Immunity; City Engineer. The City Council wishes to obtain the
immunities set forth in Government Code § 830.6 regarding the plans and construction
of the CIP projects. Accordingly, the City Council authorizes the City Engineer to
exercise discretionary approval for plans or designs for each project identified in the CIP
  1

 in advance of the construction or improvement. Such approval must conform with the
following:

  A.  The City Engineer must determine that design and plans for the CIP
  projects are consistent with the City’s standards, guidelines, practices, or
  otherwise comply with applicable law and engineering standards,
  guidelines, or practices.

  B.  Approval must be in writing and be stamped by the City Engineer while
  exercising his or her discretion in accordance with California law.

  C.  The design approval must occur before a solicitation of bids is issued in
  accordance with this Resolution and before actual construction work
  construction commences.

  D.  The City Engineer is authorized to act on the City’s behalf in approving
  any alterations or modifications of approved design and plans.

SECTION 3: Solicitation of Bids; Public Works Director. For CIP projects exceeding the
threshold in MPMC § 3.100.040 for informal bidding (at the time this Resolution was
adopted, the threshold is $200,000 or more), the Public Works Director is authorized to
solicit bids for projects identified in the CIP and in the current Budget Resolution without
additional City Council authorization. Such solicitation for bids must comply with
applicable California law including, without limitation, the Public Contract Code. The
Public Works Director is required to bring all recommendations for award to the City
Council.

SECTION 3: Electronic Signatures. This Resolution may be executed with electronic
signatures in accordance with Government Code §16.5. Such electronic signatures will
be treated in all respects as having the same effect as an original signature.

SECTION 4: Recordation. The Mayor, or presiding officer, is authorized to sign this
Resolution signifying its adoption by the City Council of the City of Monterey Park and the
City Clerk, or her duly appointed deputy, may attest thereto.

SECTION 5: Effective Date. This Resolution will become effective immediately upon
adoption and will remain effective unless repealed or superseded.

  DATE: June 18, 2024
  AGENDA ITEM NO: New Business - 5A

 TO:  The Honorable Mayor and City Council
 FROM:  Diana Garcia, Assistant City Manager
  Jessica Serrano, Community Development Director
 SUBJECT:  Consideration and possible action to adopt an urgency ordinance
  implementing interim development regulations for Saturn Park upon a
  four-fifths vote

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Adopting an Urgency Ordinance upon 4/5 vote pursuant to Government Code §
  65858 establishing a moratorium on new development within Saturn Park for 45
  days; and
  2. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
On June 5, 2024, the City Council directed that the City Manager and City Attorney
prepare a draft moratorium governing Saturn Park for consideration on the June 18th
meeting agenda. If adopted, the draft urgency ordinance would prohibit new permits being
issued for development within Saturn Park for at least 45 days. This would allow the
SPARC to receive public input regarding recommended land uses as part of the drafting
of a Saturn Park Specific Plan (“SPSP”) implementing the 2020 Land Use Element
adopted by voters via Measure JJ. The moratorium may be extended up to a total of two
years.

CEQA REVIEW:
Adopting the Urgency Ordinance is exempt from further environmental review under the
California Environmental Quality Act (California Public Resources Code §§ 21000, et
seq., “CEQA”) and CEQA Guidelines (14 California Code of Regulations §§ 15000, et
seq.) because it establishes rules and procedures for operation of existing facilities; minor
temporary use of land; minor alterations in land use; new construction of small structures;
and minor structures accessory to existing commercial facilities. The Urgency Ordinance,
therefore, is categorically exempt from further CEQA review under CEQA Guidelines §§
15301; 15303, 15304(e); 15305; and 15311. Further, the adoption of the Urgency
Ordinance is also exempt from review under CEQA pursuant to CEQA Guidelines §
15061(b)(3) because the Ordinance is for general policies and procedure-making. This
Ordinance does not authorize any new development entitlements, but simply establishes

policies and procedures for allowing the previously approved project to be constructed.
Any proposed project that will utilize the changes set forth in this Ordinance will be subject
to CEQA review as part of the entitlement review of the project. The Ordinance will not
adversely impact the environment and is therefore exempt from the provisions of CEQA.

BACKGROUND:
The City Council asked that this matter be placed on the agenda for consideration pending
the SPARC’s efforts to solicit public input for drafting the SPSP. It is anticipated that the
SPARC will wrap up its efforts in August or September 2024. Consequently, should the
City Council adopt this urgency ordinance, it may need to consider extending a
moratorium following a noticed public hearing before August 2, 2024.

As noted in the draft urgency ordinance, a review of existing zoning for Saturn Park shows
that it is inconsistent with Measure JJ that voters approved in 2020. Measure JJ adopted
the Land Use Element to the Monterey Park General Plan (the “2020 LUE”).

The 2020 LUE designates land uses in Saturn Park as “Innovation/Technology.” A
description of those land uses are included as an exhibit to this staff report. Measure JJ
specifically authorizes the City Council to adopt zoning regulations needed to implement
this land use designation.

One of the complementary land uses contemplated by the Planning Commission and the
City Council for Saturn Park is a residential component. It is anticipated that the SPARC
will consider the feasibility of this land use as it considers public input regarding the SPSP.
Residential use is desirable as it would help facilitate the City’s adherence to its Certified
Housing Element; reflects the California Legislature’s ongoing efforts to increase housing
opportunities; and implements the overall goal of the 2020 LUE as to providing flexible
zoning to improve the City’s livability.

The need for a moratorium is underscored by interest from private property owners within
Saturn Park who already filed applications with the City seeking approvals via Chapter
21.14 of the Monterey Park Municipal Code (“MPMC”). This Chapter was added by voters
in 1998 but is now inconsistent with the Monterey Park General Plan, i.e., the 2020 LUE.
For land use regulations to be legal, California law (Government Code § 65860) requires
that there be consistency between the General Plan and the City’s zoning. Voter enacted
regulations cannot overcome this requirement.1

Adopting a moratorium will provide the SPARC an opportunity to give the City Council an
informed recommendation regarding the SPSP. If adopted by a 4/5 vote of the City
Council, the urgency ordinance would impose a temporary moratorium on issuing permits
for land use entitlements within Saturn Park. The temporary moratorium would expire on
August 2, 2024 unless extended before that time.

  The City Council for the City of Monterey Park does ordain as follows:

SECTION 1: This Ordinance is adopted pursuant to Government Code §§

SECTION 2: Findings. The City Council finds, determines and declares as
follows:

  A.  The City may adopt and enforce all laws and regulations not in
  conflict with the general laws and the City holds all rights and
  powers established by California law.

  B.  On June 17, 2020, the City Council approved the Land Use
  Element to the Monterey Park General Plan (the “2020 LUE”).
  Thereafter, the 2020 LUE was placed onto the November 3, 2020
  ballot as Measure JJ. Following voter approval on November 3,
  2020, the 2020 LUE (via Ordinance No. 2198) became effective on
  December 2, 2020.

  C.  Section 3(A) of Ordinance No. 2198 authorizes the City Council to
  implement the 2020 LUE by, among other things, adopting zoning
  regulations. Section 4 of Ordinance No. 2198 provides that
  Measure JJ must be interpreted to be consistent with all applicable
  law; Section 6 of Ordinance No. 2198 provides that Measure JJ
  must be broadly construed to achieve the voter’s intent in approving
  Measure JJ.

  D.  Monterey Park Municipal Code (“MPMC”) Chapter 21.14 was
  added by Measure D on April 14, 1998 (via Ordinance No. 1933).
  Measure D provided zoning regulations for the area identified as
  McCaslin Business Park.

  E.  The Land Use Policy Map (Figure LU-3 to the 2020 LUE) renamed
  this area as “Saturn Park” with a designated land use of
  “Innovation/Technology.” Goal 25 of the 2020 LUE directs the City
  Council to revitalize Saturn Park as a destination business park for
  high-quality service industry, research and development, and

   emerging industry jobs. This directive is further refined via Policy
  Nos. 25.1 to 25.3.

F.  The 2020 LUE also provides that the City Council should ensure
  flexible zoning regulations; support local businesses; maintain a
  proactive economic development program; and invest in
  commercial corridors (Policy Nos. 1.1 to 1.4).

G.  The City’s Housing Element reflects the City’s desire to encourage
  construction of housing that is attainable for households of all
  income levels. Among other things, the City Council determined
  that the City should take proactive actions to increase the
  availability of dwelling units on underutilized properties (see, e.g.,
  Section 5(C) of Resolution No. 2022-R90, adopted November 16,
  2022).

H.  It is anticipated that the Saturn Park Advisory Review Committee
  (“SPARC”) will consider incorporating a residential component into
  the SPSP to help enhance the Innovation/Technology land use
  designation by the 2020 LUE. Among other things, this would:

  1.  Allow employees to live near their workplace, reducing
  vehicle trips.

  2.  Allow companies to offer subsidized housing as an
  employee benefit and amenity to attract talent.

  3.  Facilitate a live-work-play environment where residential,
  office, and recreational spaces coexist.

  4.  Foster closer social connections and a sense of community
  among employees who can interact more freely outside of
  work.

  5.  Align with the post-pandemic shift towards more flexible and
  hybrid workplace models.

I.  Such efforts are reflected in “real world” developments such as the
  West Edge in Los Angeles (https://westedgela.com).

J.  Additionally, the California Legislature is seeking various methods
  for promoting housing such as AB 1532 (Haney, 2023) which, were
  it approved, would allow office conversion projects by right within all
  zones. While this “Office to Housing Conversion Act” failed to
  advance within the Legislature, it represents the latest legislative
  path taken by the Legislature to encourage more housing within

  Park; the zoning regulations must be reconciled with the most

RECOMMENDATION:

  2. Appropriating $907,000 in Proposition A and C Local Return Funds from fiscal
  year 2023-2024 to continue to operate regular service hours in the current fiscal

  3. Authorizing the City Manager to execute a Second Amendment to Agreement No
  2294 with Arcadis-IBI Group Consultants, in a form approved by the City

  extends the term through June 30, 2025.
  4. Providing direction on service improvement strategies; and
  5. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
The City of Monterey Park operates a fixed-route transit service, Spirit Bus, by contract
with First Transit, Inc. Since its return to service in July 2022 following a suspension for
the Covid-19 pandemic, the City has been working with Arcadis-IBI Group Consultants
on evaluating the system’s efficiency and identifying areas of improvement. Through
additional data collection, staff has been able to compare ridership trends pre- and post-
pandemic and has a better understanding of the use of the system and its cost
effectiveness. It is recommended that City Council authorize the Fifth Amendment to
Agreement 1636-A with First Transit, Inc. to extend services to operate Spirit Bus for six
months in an amount not to exceed $1,032,270. The current Agreement will terminate on
June 30, 2024 and the Amendment will extend the term to December 31, 2024. It is further
recommended to add an option for a month-to-month term until June 30, 2025. An
extension of services with the current contractor will allow the City to develop a new
service program that would be incorporated into the RFP for the new contract for
transit/mobility services.

BACKGROUND:
The Spirit Bus service operates five local routes and the LINK shuttle service on
weekdays from 6:30 am to approximately 6:30 pm. Routes 1 to 4 are loop alignments that
link various residential neighborhoods (Brightwood, Highlands, Garvey Ranch) to
commercial areas. Route 5 provides service between Atlantic Square/East Los Angeles
College (ELAC) and the Metrolink commuter rail station at Cal State Los Angeles
(CSULA). The Link operates as a shuttle service between the LA Corporate Center and
the CSULA Metrolink Station. Due to the pandemic, service for all routes was suspended
in April 2020 and returned with reduced hours in July 2022. As of June 2023, all five
routes and the LINK have returned to their regular pre-pandemic schedule (6:30 am to
6:30 pm, Monday to Friday).

System Evaluation

In 2022, the City began working with Arcadis-IBI Group Consultants to evaluate Spirit Bus
performance by completing an assessment of existing and future conditions, new
technologies, and changing demographics. As part of this study, the City distributed a
community and student survey, hosted in-person and virtual workshops, engaged the
business community, analyzed service conditions and completed an operational analysis
of the bus system. On September 7, 2022, Arcadis-IBI presented an overview and
preliminary results of the study to City Council. At the time, the City had limited on/off
boarding data for each route. Bus stop boarding and alighting data can identify which
segments of bus routes are being used. The City has since implemented the Passio Go
app software to collect boarding and alighting data. The app also provides riders with
real-time information on when the bus would arrive at a stop to improve service reliability.

To recap the data presented by Arcadis-IBI on September 7, 2022 to the City Council,
ridership had been decreasing since 2017.

The Spirit Bus System currently consists of heavy-duty 32-foot buses and mid-sized
cutaway vehicles. The current fleet includes eight City owned buses and one spare bus
provided by First Transit. The large buses are at the end of their useful life and the mid-
sized vehicles will need to be replaced in the next two years. The proposed
implementation of new service strategies complements the timing of the purchase of
replacement vehicles. The City can expect reduced vehicle maintenance costs with the
retirement of the heavy-duty buses that may no longer be appropriate given the current
ridership levels. Large buses are costly to operate and maintain due to the increased cost
for parts ,and service. Additionally, the current buses cause excessive wear and tear on
local, residential streets. To aid in further offsetting future transportation costs, City
Council may consider supplemental revenue sources such as the use of buses, benches
and/or shelters for advertisement purposes.

Service Improvement Strategies

Based on community feedback received through survey research and community
engagement and analysis of existing Spirit Bus services, key service design issues have
been identified. Such issues include the need to simplify or redesign routes that are
presently one-way loops which can result in “out of direction travel.” Also important is
addressing connectivity to key trip attractors/generators that did not exist when the Spirit
bus routes were first designed in the 1990’s. Ancillary concerns identified include the need
for service expansion to additional days of week and earlier/later time of day; increased
service frequency; more direct/less transfers; first/last mile access; and enhanced
marketing and communications – better information on how to use transportation
services. Service improvements that are being considered include: fixed route
restructuring that reflect a more linear configuration and better connectivity to major trip

that have low ridership.

Attachment 2 - Conceptual Service Improvement Strategies identifies potential changes
to the current 5 routes:

    Route 1: Linear bi-direction route along Atlantic Blvd.

    Route 2: Linear bi-direction route along Garfield Ave.

    Route 3: Eliminate service south of Graves to Garvey Ranch and extend route east
  to Atlantic Blvd.

    Route 4: Eliminate route and provide coverage to service area through on-demand
  service

    Route 5: Expand service to connect with Metro E Line Station at Atlantic and
  Pomona and eliminate service east of Atlantic and Riggin. Provide additional
  coverage through on-demand service along Riggin Road, including service to the
  Monterey Park Marketplace Shopping Center.

Dial-a-Ride

In addition to the replacement of Spirit bus vehicles, three Dial-A-Ride vehicles that have
reached the end of their useful life are scheduled to be replaced in FY2024. The vehicles
due for replacement includes two Priuses and one Dodge minivan. Larger vehicles will
be purchased than the current Prius models. The benefit of the Priuses was the ability to
maneuver the vehicles into tight parking lots and garages and reduce travel time.
However, the drawback was limited storage for groceries for group passenger shopping
trips (e.g., Costco, Ralphs). The proposed replacement vehicles will accommodate more
passengers as well as cargo. Another improvement to Dial-A-Ride is upgrading its manual
dispatch system to a software program that can optimize routes and improve on-time
performance. The new paratransit dispatch and scheduling software will allow the current
dispatch staffing to more efficiently match customer requests to available slots and
increase the total number of passenger trips. These improvements can facilitate the
expansion of Dial-A-Ride to service residential areas that will no longer be served by the
Spirit Bus service.

Costs

The cost to operate the Spirit But is currently $108.66 per hour. Each of the 5 routes cost
the City $325,980 per year (12 hours per day, Monday to Friday).

FY2023 costs for the city’s Dial-A-Ride service is $642,775. This budget includes three
full-time drivers, dispatcher, administrative overhead, and vehicle operations and

Recommendation
At this time, staff recommends implementing the proposed service improvement
strategies through a pilot program. The pilot would include proposed restructuring of
routes, temporary elimination of Route #4, and on-demand transportation services to
service areas no longer served by Spirit Bus. To move forward with the proposed pilot
program and continue transit operations, it is recommended that the City amends its
agreement with First Transit to continue operating the fixed-route transit system for six
months - extending the term of the Agreement from June 30, 2024 to December 31, 2024.
An extension of services with the current contractor will allow the City to develop service
improvement strategies and conduct a pilot run of the proposed service(s). The Request
for Proposal (RFP) for a new contract will reflect the approved changes.

The total cost for First Transit’s Fifth Amendment is $1,939,270. A portion of this cost is
to cover regular service hours for the remaining of fiscal year 2023-2024. The Fourth
Amendment with First Transit was based on reduced service hours when service first
resumed after the pandemic. Subsequently, the City decided to return to the normal
schedule as of July 1, 2023. The additional cost to operate regular service hours until
June 30, 2024 is $907,000. For the new fiscal year, 2024 to 2025, the cost to operate the
normal schedule is $1,032,270 for the first six months. The Amendment provides an
option to continue service on a month to month basis until the end of the fiscal year (June
30, 2025).

Staff also recommends an amendment to the agreement with Arcadis-IBI Group
Consultants to extend the term of the agreement and increase the project budget by an
additional $24,665. Due to the additional data collection and analysis of services, the
consultant’s services has extended longer than originally anticipated. By amending the
contract, the City would be able to continue to work with Arcadis-IBI to develop service
recommendations and complete the RFP process for a new contract.

Design Issues

1. Routes 1-4 are designed primarily to connect residential neighborhoods to Downtown Monterey
  Park.
  •  Impedes productivity by discouraging two-way passenger traffic across the service day.
  Limited demand for AM travel away from Downtown and PM travel toward Downtown.
  •  Excessive circuity in Downtown area alignments.

2. Need to simplify or redesign Routes 1 and 2 presently operating one-way loops in opposite
  directions on similar alignments to create bi-directional service to customers.
  •  Confusing to customers because the routes are not the same and so travel times are not
  the same in opposite directions.
  •  Route 2 loop through the Monterey Highlands is a significant inconvenience to most
  customers using the route.
3. Route 4 should be modified to address Metro’s discontinuation of Route 258 service on
  Monterey Pass Road.
4. Only Route 5 connects directly to the CSULA Metrolink and Metro J (Silver) Line stations.

5. Spirit’s main transfer point at City Hall for Routes 1-4 is not served by regional bus lines.
  •  Discourages transfers between Spirit and Metro/MBL buses.
  •  Location adds travel time for transferring customers.
6. Spirit does not connect directly to the E (Gold) Line terminal station on 3rd Street west of Atlantic

7. Service to McCaslin Business Park is limited to one morning and one afternoon trip on the Route

  •  Currently designed to shuttle reverse commuters to and from the CSULA Metrolink and

8. Currently no Spirit Bus service to Marketplace Shopping Center (Costco, Home Depot,

Conceptual Service Improvement Strategies
Based on the design issues noted above, the technical team presents potential service improvement
concepts for discussion and possible further evaluation (illustrated in Exhibit 2).
Improvement concepts – A Way Forward, include:
  ▪  Consideration of route restructuring to reflect a more linear configuration and connectivity to
  major trip attractors/generators.
  ▪  Convert service to on-demand/microtransit delivery framework with consideration of:
  o Select service areas
  o Select times of day/days of week
  o Integrated with Dial-A-Ride
  o Discussions with LA Metro (possible expansion of Micro service)
These modifications were further informed by the following:
  •  Review of pre-pandemic ridership data and a comparison to ridership data gathered since all
  5 Spirit Bus routes resumed service in July 2023.
  •  Review of service cost increases and ridership/revenue decreases
  •  Community outreach and feedback gathered in 2022.

Presented for discussion, conceptual service improvement strategies are listed by route below.
Route 1
Ridership is down along the downtown segment from 75-100 riders per day pre-pandemic to about
50 riders per day in October 2023. This is still one of the higher ridership segments. Other segments
have recovered to pre-pandemic ranges but with lower ridership. Confusion in directionality for
passengers suggests route could be restructured from a one-way loop to a linear route along
Atlantic.
  •  Restructure service routing to accommodate bi-directional travel.
