Route 2
Ridership along the Atlantic Boulevard, Downtown, and Garfield segments represent only 24-40% of
pre-pandemic ridership numbers. Ridership along the Hillside and Riggin St. segments has
recovered but remains low at 13-18 passengers per day on average. Confusion in directionality for
passengers suggests route could be restructured from a one-way loop to a linear route along
Garfield.
  •  Restructure service routing to accommodate bi-directional travel.
  •  Eliminate residential loop north of Floral Drive to improve travel times and reduce circuity.

Route 3
Route 3 ridership has returned to within pre-pandemic ranges along all segments and carries 83
passengers per day in the downtown core as of October 2023. However, the reservoir loop impedes
two-way passenger travel and is the lowest ridership along the route at 35 passengers per day.
  •  Eliminate of fixed-route service south of Graves Avenue.
  •  Redirect current route to travel north on Alhambra Avenue from Graves Avenue to provide
  new service to relatively dense residential neighborhoods and increase service frequency.
  •  Provide on-demand ride hail service within a defined zone south of Graves Avenue to
  provide more flexible travel options to existing passengers.
  •  Potentially extend existing route farther east to Atlantic Avenue in combination with service
  changes proposed for Route 4 (below).

Route 4
No segment along Route 4 is generating more than 57% of ridership compared to pre-pandemic.
Monterey Pass and Corporate Center segments are getting less than 5 passengers per day.
Downtown loop is duplicated by other routes.
  •  Eliminate existing fixed route transit service.
  •  Provide on-demand ride hail service within a defined zone along Monterey Pass Road and in
  the residential neighborhoods to the north that are currently served by Route 4.
  •  Provide connectivity through on-demand service to CSULA Metrolink and Metro J (Silver)
  Line stations.

Route 5
Data by stop is limited due to unresolved issues with onboard technology. Overall data by route
shows an average of 21 passengers per day along the whole route in October 2023. Ridership along
E Riggin St. and McCaslin Business Park segments was low in 2019 and is now likely lower. Route
5 does provide a key connection to CSULA Metrolink Station and could be altered to serve ELAC
transit center and Metro E Line.
  •  Eliminate existing fixed route transit service east of Atlantic and Riggin that currently
  operates for only two daily trips.
  •  Expand service to connect with Metro E Line Atlantic Station/Kaiser Permanente East Los
  Angeles Medical Offices.

  •  Expand existing Monterey Park Dial-a-Ride service to allow trips within a defined service
  area along Riggin Road and providing connectivity to the southeastern corner of the city,

These modifications are designed to improve service by replacing poorly performing, infrequent, and
circuitous routes with more flexible service that still meets the needs of residents that live in areas
that are not well suited to fixed route transit. It would also provide a new connection for residents to
regional transit and to an important commercial destination and improve service frequency for Route
3 while adding service through a relatively densely populated neighborhood.

Fiscal Impact
As previously mentioned, the conceptual service improvement strategies contained herein are
presented for discussion and possible further evaluation.
If an appetite to advance the further evaluation of Spirit Bus service improvement strategies, it is
anticipated that alternate service delivery scenarios including levels of service for route restructuring
(including schedules, frequency, and span of service) and the deployment of on-demand services
will be commensurate with available fiscal resources.
For example, if the Route 4 were discontinued, the approximate $320k for this current route
operations could be reallocated to on-demand services.

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Whether to direct the City Attorney to request a California Attorney General
  Opinion regarding the legality of “claw machines”; and
  2. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

BACKGROUND:
In May, the City’s Community Development Department received a request from a
business owner to process a conditional use permit (“CUP”) to open an arcade utilizing a
“claw machine” (see attached description from Wikipedia). Because the “claw machine”
appeared to require a separate permit by Monterey Park Municipal Code (“MPMC”)
Chapter 5.20, the Community Development Director asked me to review the MPMC to
determine whether there was a more expedient method of addressing the game permit
requirement.

A review of MPMC Chapter 5.20 shows that those regulations were adopted by the City
Council in the late 1950s (see, e.g., Ordinance No. 874, adopted November 23, 1959).
Most local gambling regulations were superseded by California law in the late 1990s when
the Legislature enacted a comprehensive regulatory scheme for gambling that is enforced
by the Bureau of Gambling Control. That Bureau is a division of the California Attorney
General’s Office. Generally, local agencies may only regulate bingo and card rooms; all
other gaming is regulated by the California Penal Code. With that understanding, I
reviewed the Penal Code requirements as to claw machines.

In doing so, I found the attached Law Enforcement Advisory dated November 1, 2010
issued by the Bureau of Gambling Control. It identifies claw machines as a “[c]ommon
type” of illegal gambling device. Based upon the Police Chief’s information from
representatives of the Bureau of Gambling Control, this 2010 Advisory continues to be in
effect. Consequently, a claw machine is classified as an illegal gambling device. As a
result, the City cannot process the CUP application by the arcade owner: the City cannot
approve a CUP for illegal activity.

 NUMBER 10  LAW ENFORCEMENT ADVISORY  NOVEMBER 1, 2010

  Illegal Gambling Devices

  The Bureau of Gambling Control (Bureau) provides this advisory regarding illegal gambling
devices in response to inquiries from local law enforcement agencies, inquiries from state agencies
including the California State Lottery and the California Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control, and
from the Bureau’s observations in the field. This advisory also addresses misrepresentations contained in
documents circulating in the industry that are fraudulently prepared to appear as though they were issued
by this office. As a general matter, most, if not all, gambling devices—other than those operating in
California Tribal Casinos—that a person pays to play, and that offer anything of value for playing, are
illegal devices. Common types of illegal devices include coin pushers, electronic trivia games that
include any element of chance, claw machines, traditional slot machines, and slot machines that purport to
have a skill element.

  The attached flow chart outlines the steps for determining what is an illegal gambling device. (See
attachment #1.)

  Illegal Gambling Devices

  California’s gambling device statutes are broad in their coverage and prohibit any person from
owning, renting, or possessing illegal gambling devices. (Penal Code, §§ 330a, 330b, 330.1.) An illegal
gambling device has three features:

  1. It is a machine, apparatus, or device (coin operation is not required);
  2. Something of value is given to play the device; and
  3. The player has the opportunity to receive something of value by any element of hazard or
  chance (“something of value” is not limited to coins, bills, or tokens—it also includes free
  replays, additional playing time, redemption tickets, gift cards, game credits, or anything else
  with a value, monetary or otherwise.) (Penal Code, §§ 330a, 330b & 330.1.)

  In addition, if a device can readily be converted to have the features of an illegal gambling device,
(as listed in 1, 2, and 3 above), it is an illegal device. (Penal Code, § 330b(d).)

  Page 439 of 459
 Page 2 Number 10  Law Enforcement Advisory
  Narrowly Defined Amusement Device Exception

  Devices that fall within the definition of an illegal gambling device above may nevertheless
qualify for the “pinball” or “amusement device” exception if they meet the narrow requirements set forth
in the provisions of Penal Code section 330b, subdivision (f), and section 330.5. A gaming device
qualifies for the amusement device exception, and therefore is lawful, if it:

  1. Provides an opportunity to win nothing other than additional or free play; and
  2. Is predominantly a game of skill.

  A lawful device is one that is predominately a game of skill (as are most arcade pinball
machines), on which what can be won is limited to additional chances or free plays. If, however, the
player has paid to play and can win something other than additional plays, such as food, toys, or other
prizes, the machine does not qualify for the amusement device exception and is an illegal gambling
device. As an additional example, a coin pusher is an illegal gambling device, whether or not it purports
to have an element of skill, because the player can win coins by playing.

  California Tribal Casinos

  California Tribal Casinos are permitted to operate slot machines pursuant to the terms of
approved Tribal-State Compacts and California law.

  False Representations Regarding the Legality of Devices

  The Bureau has obtained memorandums that falsely purport to be issued by the Office of the
Attorney General claiming that coin pusher games are legal as games of skill. (See attachment #2.) In
addition, the Bureau has received information that some manufacturers and vendors are misrepresenting
the Penal Code’s narrow “amusement device” exception in an attempt to portray their gambling devices
as compliant with California law.

  The Attorney General’s Office has not approved any such device for play in California, nor
issued any opinion or statement regarding the legality of any such device on the basis of the
predominance of skill. The Bureau notes, however, that its field operations have detected a growing
number of gaming devices throughout California that are illegal because they offer prizes and are not
otherwise exempted from the prohibitions of the Penal Code.

  The purpose of an advisory is informational. An advisory does not constitute legal advice.

  A claw machine is a type of arcade game. Modern claw
  machines are upright cabinets with glass boxes that are lit from
  the inside and have a joystick-controlled claw at the top, which
  is coin-operated and positioned over a pile of prizes, dropped
  into the pile, and picked up to unload the prize or lack thereof

  are also known as skill cranes, claw cranes, and crane
  games, and are known as UFO catchers in Japan due to the

  The earliest claw machines are believed to have been created in

  build the Panama Canal, while the first patented claw machine,

  North America
  The passing of the Johnson Act by Congress in 1951, which prohibited the transfer of electronic
  gambling devices across state lines, led to Miami Diggers at carnivals being destroyed by operators
  or seized by government officials. Carnival owner Lee Moss organized other carnival owners
  together to protest against the classification of the diggers as gambling machines. Because of this, a
  compromise was soon reached that allowed carnival owners to keep the diggers but required them
  to be manually operated with no coin slot and prizes that were not money and worth one dollar or
  less, while the government would tax each machine US$10. Regulations loosened in 1973 due to
  the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) abandoning the Johnson Act.[2] As of 2015, state
  regulations generally require that claw machines contain less valuable prizes.[31] Most states
  exempt claw machines from their gambling laws.[49]

  In New Jersey, claw machines are regulated by the Legalized Games of Chance Control
  Commission. In 2016, New Jersey Senator Nicholas Scutari proposed legislation that would add

  game shall not be considered as a game of skill and science, but shall be considered as a game of chance; but expressly not including
  any and all athletic games not played upon a table, cabinet or mechanical device and furthermore expressly excluding: billiards and
  pool games played upon billiard and pool tables of standard size and dimensions, the games of chess, checkers, all legal playing card
  games of skill and science, and athletic sporting events;

  "Horse racing machine" means any mechanically operated amusement machine or device contrived to simulate in miniature the running of a
  horse race or any other race run by beasts, human beings or machines, or which is contrived to put in motion any number of objects or symbols
  which then do, or appear to, run or move against each other in the manner of a miniature race, or which is designed to represent by symbols,
  the running of any race and the order of the finish thereof;

  "Marble game" means any table, cabinet or stand equipped for the playing of a game whereby marbles or balls are, with the aid of a mechanical
  plunger or other affixed device, propelled, released, shot or rolled so as to drop or come to rest in holes, slots, cups or traps, resulting in a score
  or tally being electrically or otherwise registered or shown which score or tally depends upon the course followed or point reached by the marble
  or ball or upon the contact points touched by it along its course, or upon any combination of such factors;

  "Pin game" means any table, cabinet or mechanism equipped for the playing of any game whereby any marble, ball, pellet or other moving
  object is propelled, released, rolled or shot along, over or above a surface set with pins, pegs or other obstructions or irregularities which deflect
  or impede the course of the moving object or which may divert or direct it beyond the control of the player.

  RESOLUTION NO.

  A RESOLUTION OF THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF MONTEREY
  PARK, CALIFORNIA, DECLARING AND RECOGNIZING JUNE 24-28,
  2024, AS NATIONAL BOYS & GIRLS CLUB WEEK

  BE IT RESOLVED by the Council of the City of Monterey Park as follows:

SECTION 1: The City Council finds as follows:

  A. The Boys & Girls Club of America had its origins in 1860 when four women (Mary
  Goodwin, Alice Goodwin, Elizabeth Hammersley, and Louisa Bushnell) organized
  their first Boys Club with the belief that boys who roamed the streets should have
  a positive alternative. This first Boys Club focused on capturing boys’ interests,
  improving their behavior, and supporting their aspirations and goals.

  B. Motivated by cultivating character development for youth and teens, several Boys
  Clubs decided to affiliate in 1906 and the Federated Boys Clubs was formed in
  Boston with 53 member organizations. This marked the start of a nationwide
  movement and their national organization.

  C. In 1990, the national organization’s name was officially changed to Boys & Girls
  Clubs of America to recognize the fact that girls are also a part of the cause. As of
  today, Boys & Girls Clubs of America serve over 3.3 million kids through
  memberships and community outreach programs in more than 5,200 Club
  facilities.

  D. The Boys & Girls Clubs of America’s mission is to enable all young people,
  especially those who need them the most, to reach their full potential as productive,
  caring, responsible citizens. Young individuals need safe, welcoming places where
  they can learn, grow, and thrive, and the Boys & Girls Clubs of America provides
  that access to life-shaping experiences.

  E. National Boys & Girls Club Week has been celebrated since 1941 and recognizes
  the invaluable service all Clubs bring to our communities. These Clubs pave the
  road for great futures for every young person who enters their doors and this week
  encourages community members to visit their local Club and get involved.

  F. Monterey Park is home to the Boys & Girls Club of West San Gabriel Valley which
  was established in 1972 by Dr. Friedrich Thomas. The Boys & Girls Club of West
  San Gabriel Valley has been a cornerstone of the community and provides a safe,
  structured environment for young people after school, during holidays, and on
  summer vacation.

  G. Without safe and supervised after-school activities, boys and girls in every
  community are left to find their own recreation and companionship in the streets.
  Young people need to know that someone cares about them and the Boys & Girls

  Page 456 of 459
   Club of West San Gabriel Valley has been offering these opportunities for more
  than 50 years in Monterey Park.

  H. The Boys & Girls Club of West San Gabriel Valley is a safe place to learn and
  grow, all while having fun and promoting social, educational, health, leadership,
  and character development of boys and girls during critical periods of their lives.

  I. The City Council of Monterey Park supports all youth and teens in reaching their
  full potential and is committed to promoting safe, positive, healthy, and inclusive
  environments that catalyze meaningful change.

  J. The City Council of Monterey Park hereby proclaims June 24-28, 2024, as National
  Boys & Girls Club Week and encourages all community members to celebrate by
  observing and participating in nationwide activities that include engaging with their
  local Club, learning about their mission, and discovering various programs that
  promote building a brighter future for our youth.

  RESOLUTION NO.

  A RESOLUTION OF THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF MONTEREY
  PARK, CALIFORNIA, DECLARING AND RECOGNIZING JUNE 23, 2024,
  AS THE 42ND ANNIVERSARY OF THE DEATH OF VINCENT JEN CHIN

  BE IT RESOLVED by the Council of the City of Monterey Park as follows:

SECTION 1: The City Council finds as follows:

  A. June 23, 2024, marks the 42nd anniversary of the passing of Vincent Jen Chin, a
  United States citizen of Chinese descent who was tragically murdered in a racially
  motivated assault in Michigan during the deindustrialization of the Midwest.

  B. During the economic recession in the early 1980s, the decline of the auto industry
  provoked resentment toward imported Japanese cars in Detroit which was the
  center of the automotive industry in the United States.

  C. The economic challenges in Detroit resulted in strong anti-Japanese sentiments.
  Many American motor executives, politicians, unions, and autoworkers took out
  their frustration against anything and anyone they thought could be Japanese
  including acts of vandalism against Japanese cars, threats against Japanese car
  owners, disparaging signs, and attempts to burn the Japanese flag in protest.

  D. Unfortunately, the animosity also extended to other Asian Americans who were
  lumped together as “perpetual foreigners” and invoked racial rhetoric that turned
  many to violence.

  E. On June 19, 1982, Chin was chased down and beaten with a baseball bat by two
  men who accused him of being responsible for the loss of automobile
  manufacturing jobs in the United States while celebrating his upcoming wedding
  with friends in the Detroit area. Chin was rushed to a hospital and was comatose
  on arrival, however, he never regained consciousness and died four days later on
  June 23, 1982.

  F. Chin’s killers were found guilty of manslaughter and sentenced to three years of
  probation and a $3,000 fine, never serving a day in jail for Chin’s murder.

  G. The tragedy of Chin’s death became a primary catalyst for a unified, pan-ethnic
  Asian American and Pacific Islander (AAPI) movement and united people from all
  communities to fight against hate. The lessons of building solidarity and unity to
  obtain justice for Chin brought people together to counter division and hate and
  inspired older and younger generations to demand positive change.

  H. Today, the fight against anti-Asian hate continues, but also includes other ongoing
  issues that affect the AAPI community such as profiling, xenophobia, bullying,
  immigration, and negative media portrayals.

  Page 458 of 459
   I. According to the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), hate crimes reported by law
  enforcement agencies rose from more than 8,000 in 2020 to nearly 11,000 in 2021.
  Anti-Asian hate crimes increased by 124% in 2020 and 339% in 2021.

  J. Although the FBI has reported a 33% decrease in anti-Asian hate crimes for the
  first time from 2021 to 2022, anti-Asian hate continues to this day. Community
  members are urged to continue to raise awareness of anti-Asian hate crimes and
  to increase tolerance, safety, and belonging among the AAPI community.

  K. The City of Monterey Park recognizes the significance of Vincent Chins’ death as
  an important time to reflect on the dangers of xenophobia and scapegoating of
  Asian and Asian-American communities. Chin’s death left an immense impact on
  Asian American communities locally and nationwide and the City of Monterey Park
  encourages the public to foster dialogue, share resources, and learn more about
  what they can do to combat anti-Asian hate.

  L. The City Council of Monterey Park mourns all those who have lost their lives to anti-
  Asian hate and declares and recognizes June 23, 2024, as the 42nd anniversary of
  the passing of Vincent Jen Chin.

  Senate Bill 1 (SB1), the Road Repair and Accountability Act of 2017, addresses
  the significant multi-modal transportation funding shortfall statewide. As of
  November 2017, portions of SB1 revenues are deposited into a Road Maintenance
  and Rehabilitation Account (RMRA) and made available to eligible cities and
  counties, which must comply with RMRA funding requirements as determined by
  the California Transportation Commission (CTC).

  RMRA funds made available for the Local Streets and Roads Funding Program
  are prioritized for expenditure on basic road maintenance and rehabilitation
  projects, and on critical safety projects. The CTC provided a number of example
  projects and uses for RMRA funding that includes, but are not limited to, the
  following: road maintenance and rehabilitation, safety projects, railroad grade
  separations, complete streets components (including active transportation
  purposes, pedestrian and bicycle safety projects, transit facilities, and drainage
  and stormwater capture projects in conjunction with any other allowable project),
  and traffic control devices.

  Action Taken: The City Council adopted Resolution No. 2024-R46 identifying a
  street maintenance project to be included in the FY 2024-25 budget and funded
  with Road Maintenance and Rehabilitation Act (RMRA) funds, in a form approved

CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act):
Adopting the Urgency Ordinance is exempt from further environmental review
under the California Environmental Quality Act (California Public Resources Code
§§ 21000, et seq., “CEQA”) and CEQA Guidelines (14 California Code of
Regulations §§ 15000, et seq.) because it establishes rules and procedures for
operation of existing facilities; minor temporary use of land; minor alterations in
land use; new construction of small structures; and minor structures accessory to
existing commercial facilities. The Urgency Ordinance, therefore, is categorically
exempt from further CEQA review under CEQA Guidelines §§ 15301; 15303,
15304(e); 15305; and 15311. Further, the adoption of the Urgency Ordinance is
also exempt from review under CEQA pursuant to CEQA Guidelines § 15061(b)(3)
because the Ordinance is for general policies and procedure-making. This
Ordinance does not authorize any new development entitlements, but simply
establishes policies and procedures for allowing the previously approved project
to be constructed. Any proposed project that will utilize the changes set forth in this
Ordinance will be subject to CEQA review as part of the entitlement review of the
project. The Ordinance will not adversely impact the environment and is therefore
exempt from the provisions of CEQA.

  “CLAW MACHINES” WITHIN THE CITY OF MONTEREY PARK

  In May, the City’s Community Development Department received a request from a
  business owner to process a conditional use permit (“CUP”) to open an arcade
  utilizing a “claw machine” (see attached description from Wikipedia). Because the
  “claw machine” appeared to require a separate permit by Monterey Park Municipal
  Code (“MPMC”) Chapter 5.20, the Community Development Director asked City
  Attorney Berger to review the MPMC to determine whether there was a more
  expedient method of addressing the game permit requirement.

  This item was heard after Item No. 5A.

  Action Taken: The City Council directed the City Attorney to request a California
  Attorney General Opinion regarding the legality of “claw machines.”
